summary30Seconds: Cropping Seasons: Kharif (June-Sept; rice, cotton, jute), Rabi (Oct-March; wheat, gram, mustard), Zaid (April-June; watermelon, vegetables).
Major Crops: Rice (2nd after China, aus/aman/boro in WB); Wheat (rabi, Punjab/Haryana/UP); Arabica coffee from Yemen grown in Nilgiri hills (Karnataka, Kerala, TN).
Rainwater Harvesting: Neeru-Meeru (Andhra Pradesh), Arvary Pani Sansad (Alwar, Rajasthan), mandatory rooftop rainwater harvesting in Tamil Nadu.
Mineral Belts: North-Eastern Plateau (Chhota Nagpur - 'Ruhr of India'); Coal: 98% Gondwana (Damodar, Son, Mahanadi; Jharia, Raniganj) vs Tertiary (Assam, Meghalaya; Lignite at Neyveli, TN).
Indira Gandhi Canal: Takes off from Harike Barrage (Satlaj-Beas confluence) to green the Thar Desert.

coreConcepts.title: 1. Land Resources & Indian Cropping Seasons
coreConcepts.content:
Agricultural activity in India follows three distinct cropping seasons:

• **Kharif Season (June to September)**:
  - Coincides with the South-West Monsoon.
  - Major crops: **Rice (Paddy), Cotton, Jute, Jowar, Bajra, Tur (Arhar)**.
  - In West Bengal, farmers grow three crops of rice in a year: **Aus** (autumn), **Aman** (winter), and **Boro** (summer).

• **Rabi Season (October to March / April)**:
  - Begins with the onset of winter and harvested in spring.
  - Major crops: **Wheat, Gram, Rapeseed, Mustard, Barley, Peas**.
  - Success in Punjab and Haryana is aided by western temperate cyclonic disturbances (Mahawat).

• **Zaid Season (April to June)**:
  - Short summer cropping season between rabi harvest and kharif sowing.
  - Major crops: **Watermelon, Muskmelon, Cucumber, Vegetables, and Fodder crops**.
ncertPointers: Aus, Aman, and Boro are the three rice crops grown in West Bengal and Assam.
Mustard and Gram are Rabi crops; Cotton and Jute are Kharif crops.

coreConcepts.title: 2. Water Resources & Watershed Management Initiatives
coreConcepts.content:
India accounts for ~2.45% of world surface area, 4% of world water resources, but ~17.5% of world population.
• **Groundwater Utilisation**: Extremely high in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, and Tamil Nadu (>85% groundwater overexploited). Moderate in Gujarat, UP, Bihar; low in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and North-Eastern states.
• **Water Pollution**: Domestic sewage and industrial effluents heavily contaminate river stretches; the **Ganga** (Kanpur to Varanasi) and the **Yamuna** (Delhi to confluence with Chambal) are the most critically polluted.

• **Community Watershed & Water Harvesting Success Stories**:
  - **Haryali**: Central government sponsored watershed development project implemented by Gram Panchayats.
  - **Neeru-Meeru (Water and You)**: Popular participatory water conservation programme launched in **Andhra Pradesh**.
  - **Arvary Pani Sansad**: People's water parliament in **Alwar, Rajasthan**, which constructed Johads (earthen check dams).
  - **Tamil Nadu**: The first state in India to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all residential houses.
ncertPointers: Match-the-following: Neeru-Meeru -> Andhra Pradesh; Arvary Pani Sansad -> Alwar, Rajasthan.
Tamil Nadu is the state where rooftop rainwater harvesting is legally mandatory.

coreConcepts.title: 3. Mineral Belts & Fossil Fuels of India
coreConcepts.content:
India's minerals are concentrated in three major geographic belts:

• **1. North-Eastern Plateau Belt**:
  - Covers Chhota Nagpur (Jharkhand), Odisha plateau, and West Bengal.
  - India's richest mineral belt; contains vast reserves of **iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite, and mica** ('Ruhr of India').

• **2. South-Western Plateau Belt**:
  - Extends over Karnataka, Goa, and contiguous Tamil Nadu and Kerala uplands.
  - Rich in **ferrous metals (iron ore in Bellary-Hospet, Kudremukh), bauxite**, and high-grade limestone. Lacks coal except lignite at **Neyveli**.

• **3. North-Western Belt**:
  - Extends along the Aravalli in Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat.
  - Famous for **non-ferrous minerals**: copper (Khetri), zinc, lead (Zawar), marble, granite, and sandstone.

• **Coal Resources**:
  - **Gondwana Coal (98% of reserves)**: Formed 250 million years ago; bituminous metallurgical grade coal. Major fields: **Jharia** (largest coalfield), **Raniganj** (oldest coalfield), Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura in Damodar Valley, Son, Mahanadi, Godavari valleys.
  - **Tertiary Coal (2% of reserves)**: Formed 15-50 million years ago; high sulphur, young coal. Found in Assam (Makum, Nazira), Meghalaya (Cherrapunji, Daranggiri), Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, and Jammu & Kashmir.
  - **Lignite (Brown Coal)**: Mined at **Neyveli in Cuddalore district of Tamil Nadu** (used for thermal power generation).

• **Petroleum**:
  - **Digboi (Assam)**: Oldest oil producing field in India (1889).
  - **Mumbai High**: Offshore oilfield discovered in 1974, situated 160 km off the Mumbai coast in the Arabian Sea; biggest domestic producer.
  - **Gujarat**: Ankleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Lunej.
ncertPointers: Jharia is the largest coalfield; Raniganj is the oldest.
Digboi is the oldest oilfield; Mumbai High is offshore.
Neyveli lignite is in Tamil Nadu.

coreConcepts.title: 4. Target Area Planning & Indira Gandhi Canal Project
coreConcepts.content:
Target area programmes focus on lagging and ecologically fragile regions:
• **Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP)**: Initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan to generate employment and restore ecological balance in arid zones.
• **Hill Area Development Programme (HADP)**: Initiated during Fifth Five Year Plan covering 15 districts (nilgiris, mikir hills, etc.).

• **Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Project**:
  - Conceived by **Kanwar Sain** in 1948; launched in March 1958.
  - Takes off from **Harike Barrage** in Punjab at the confluence of the **Satlaj and Beas rivers**.
  - Runs parallel to the Pakistan border for ~650 km through Rajasthan.
  - **Stage I**: Covers Ganganagar, Hanumangarh, and Bikaner districts.
  - **Stage II**: Extends through Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, and Churu.
  - Transformed parched desert into agricultural land (wheat, cotton, mustard, groundnut), but excessive irrigation caused serious **waterlogging and soil salinisation**.
ncertPointers: Canal takes off from Harike Barrage (Satlaj + Beas confluence).
Kanwar Sain was the vision engineer behind the canal in 1948.

workedExamples.question:
The Indira Gandhi Canal originates at which barrage, located at the confluence of which two rivers?
(A) Bhakra Barrage at the confluence of Ravi and Beas
(B) Harike Barrage at the confluence of Satlaj and Beas
(C) Nangal Barrage on the Satlaj River
(D) Pong Dam on the Beas River

options.text: Bhakra Barrage at the confluence of Ravi and Beas
Harike Barrage at the confluence of Satlaj and Beas
Nangal Barrage on the Satlaj River
Pong Dam on the Beas River

solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Refer to the section on 'Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context' in NCERT.
Step 2: The Indira Gandhi Canal (previously Rajasthan Canal) originates at the Harike Barrage in Punjab.
Step 3: Harike Barrage is built at the confluence of the Satlaj and Beas rivers.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Refer to the section on 'Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context' in NCERT.
Step 2: The Indira Gandhi Canal (previously Rajasthan Canal) originates at the Harike Barrage in Punjab.
Step 3: Harike Barrage is built at the confluence of the Satlaj and Beas rivers.

workedExamples.question:
Which of the following is the oldest oil-producing region in India?
(A) Mumbai High
(B) Ankleshwar
(C) Digboi
(D) Krishna-Godavari Basin
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Check petroleum fields in NCERT India: People and Economy Ch 7.
Step 2: Digboi in Assam was discovered in 1889 and is the oldest oilfield in India.
Step 3: Mumbai High was discovered later in 1974.

howCuetAsksThis.typicalStem: Match the watershed harvesting programme with its state: Neeru-Meeru, Arvary Pani Sansad.
howCuetAsksThis.strategy: Neeru-Meeru belongs to Andhra Pradesh; Arvary Pani Sansad was in Alwar, Rajasthan.

howCuetAsksThis.typicalStem: About 98% of the coal reserves of India belong to which geological age?
howCuetAsksThis.strategy: 98% belongs to Gondwana coal fields formed 250 million years ago, located primarily in the Damodar, Son, Mahanadi, and Godavari valleys.

commonTraps.misconception: Thinking Tertiary coal accounts for the majority of India's reserves.
commonTraps.whyWrong: Tertiary coal accounts for only ~2% of reserves; 98% is Gondwana coal.
commonTraps.trapOptionExample: Option stating Tertiary coal forms 80% of Indian coal.

commonTraps.misconception: Believing Indira Gandhi Canal originated from Bhakra Dam.
commonTraps.whyWrong: The canal originates downstream at the Harike Barrage where Satlaj and Beas converge, not at Bhakra Dam.
commonTraps.correctUnderstanding: Origin point is strictly Harike Barrage.
commonTraps.trapOptionExample: Stating canal originates from Bhakra Nangal Dam.

practiceQuestions.question: In West Bengal, farmers grow three crops of rice in a year called:
practiceQuestions.explanation: In West Bengal and Assam, the three seasonal rice crops grown within a single agricultural year are Aus, Aman, and Boro.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is the largest coalfield in India in terms of reserves?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Jharia in Jharkhand is the largest coalfield in India, possessing the most valuable metallurgical coking coal reserves.

practiceQuestions.question:
Assertion (A): Excessive canal irrigation in the Indira Gandhi Canal command area has resulted in environmental problems.
Reason (R): Intensive water application in an arid region with poor drainage has led to twin menaces of waterlogging and soil salinisation.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

practiceQuestions.explanation: Over-irrigation in sandy desert soils with impermeable hard pans underneath caused the groundwater table to rise, inducing waterlogging and salinisation.

practiceQuestions.question: The 'Neeru-Meeru' (Water and You) programme is a watershed management and water harvesting initiative of which state?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Neeru-Meeru was launched in Andhra Pradesh to undertake community water conservation through excavation of percolation tanks and check dams.

practiceQuestions.question:
Match List-I (Mineral / Energy Resource) with List-II (Key Indian Location):
List-I:
p. Lignite coal
q. Oldest oilfield
r. Copper reserves
s. Largest offshore petroleum
List-II:
1. Digboi (Assam)
2. Mumbai High
3. Neyveli (Tamil Nadu)
4. Khetri (Rajasthan)
Select the correct option:
practiceQuestions.explanation: p-3 (Lignite = Neyveli), q-1 (Oldest oil = Digboi), r-4 (Copper = Khetri), s-2 (Offshore oil = Mumbai High).

practiceQuestions.question: Which Indian state was the first to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses across the state?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting legally mandatory for all existing and new structures.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following crops is a Kharif crop in North India but a Rabi crop in South India?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sesamum (Til) is grown as a Kharif crop in North India and as a Rabi crop in South India.

practiceQuestions.question: The Harike Barrage is situated at the confluence of which two rivers?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Harike Barrage is constructed at the confluence of the Satlaj and Beas rivers in Punjab.

practiceQuestions.question: What proportion of India's total coal reserves belongs to the Gondwana geological formation?
practiceQuestions.explanation: About 98% of Indian coal reserves are Gondwana coal, located primarily in peninsular river valleys.

practiceQuestions.question: In which year was the Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) initiated in India?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Drought Prone Area Programme was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan to create employment and restore ecological balance.
